item.title: The AI Agent Framework Landscape
item.description:
Simple definition#

An agent framework is a library or SDK that implements the plumbing every agent needs — the loop that calls the model, executes tools and feeds results back — plus state, memory, multi-agent coordination, human-in-the-loop, guardrails and tracing. You write the instructions, tools and business logic; the framework runs them.

item.title: What Is an AI Agent?
item.description:
Simple definition#

An AI agent is a system where an LLM decides what to do next, does it by calling tools, observes the result, and repeats until the goal is reached or it must stop.

A chatbot answers. An agent acts: it can look up an order, check a policy, issue a refund, and email the customer — choosing the steps itself.

item.title: From Generative to Agentic AI: Five Levels, SPAR and the Three Keystones
item.description:
Simple definition#

Generative AI produces content when asked. Agentic AI pursues a goal: it plans, uses tools, takes actions across systems, remembers, and improves from results — with as little human prompting as the task allows.

item.title: Python and TypeScript Agent Frameworks
item.description:
How to read this page#

Each profile answers the same questions: what is the core idea, what does minimal code look like, what is it good at, and what should you watch out for. Code is deliberately minimal and uses a placeholder MODEL; check each project’s documentation for current model identifiers and options.

item.title: Tool Calling (Function Calling)
item.description:
Simple definition#

Tool calling (also called function calling) lets an LLM ask your application to run a function. You describe the available tools; the model replies with “call get_order with {"orderId": "8812"}”; your code runs it and sends the result back; the model continues.

item.title: Agent Planning, Tool Selection and Failure Modes
item.description:
Simple definition#

An agent is defined by two things: the environment it operates in and the tools it can use. Planning is how it turns a goal into a sequence of tool calls; reflection is how it notices mistakes and corrects them.

item.title: Model Context Protocol (MCP)
item.description:
Simple definition#

The Model Context Protocol (MCP) is an open standard for connecting AI applications to tools and data. An MCP server exposes capabilities — tools to call, resources to read, prompt templates to use — and any MCP-compatible AI application can discover and use them.

item.title: Agentic Workflow Patterns
item.description:
Simple definition#

Agentic patterns are reusable shapes for combining LLM calls, tools and code — the “design patterns” of AI systems. Most production systems are a composition of a few of them. They range from fully code-controlled workflows to fully model-controlled agents.

item.title: Multi-Agent Systems
item.description:
Simple definition#

A multi-agent system splits work among several agents, each with its own instructions, tools and context, which coordinate to reach a goal. It is the AI equivalent of a team: a lead delegates to specialists.

item.title: Agent Memory, State and Durable Execution
item.description:
Simple definition#

LLMs are stateless: each call knows only what is in its prompt. Memory is everything your system stores and feeds back so an agent can continue a conversation, remember a user’s preferences, learn from past cases, and resume a long task after a crash.

item.title: Agent Reliability, Guardrails and Evaluation
item.description:
Simple definition#

Agent reliability is the engineering that makes an agent do the right thing consistently, stop when it should, and fail safely when it cannot succeed. It combines guardrails (prevent bad actions), budgets (bound cost and time), evaluation (measure behaviour before and after release) and observability (see what happened).

item.title: The Agent Protocol Stack: MCP, A2A, AG-UI, Agent Skills and AGENTS.md
item.description:
Simple definition#

Agents need to talk to three kinds of counterpart: tools and data, other agents, and people through a user interface. Since 2024 an open standard has emerged for each, plus two lightweight file conventions for giving agents know-how and instructions:

item.title: Agent Harnesses, Skills and Long-Running Agents
item.description:
Simple definition#

An agent harness is everything around the model that turns it into a working agent: the loop, tools, permissions, context management, memory files, sub-agents, skills, checkpoints and verification. Two agents using the same model can perform very differently because of their harnesses — which is why “harness engineering” became a discipline of its own in 2025–2026.

item.title: Computer-Use and Browser Agents
item.description:
Simple definition#

A computer-use agent operates software the way a person does: it looks at the screen (screenshots or the page structure), decides what to click or type, performs the action, and repeats. Browser agents are the web-only variant. They let agents work with applications that have no API.

item.title: Agent Identity and Access Control
item.description:
Simple definition#

Agent identity and access control answers three questions for every action an agent takes: who is acting (the agent, the user, or both), what are they allowed to do, and how can we prove later what happened. Agents are a new kind of non-human identity that often act on behalf of a human, so classic service-account thinking is not enough.

item.title: A Practical Playbook for Building AI Agents: Opportunity Scoring and the A.G.E.N.T. Framework
item.description:
Simple definition#

This playbook covers the practical path from “we should use agents” to an agent that works in production: find the right opportunity, score and prioritise it, design the agent with a structured framework, and implement it with principles that avoid the most common failures.
